name: 03b_mixed_english_class

context.subject: Angličtina
context.details: English-language class, the teacher teaches in English with Czech asides to explain. Students are B1.

transcript:
[Část 1]
Good morning everyone, good morning, sit down please, yes, you too Honzo, put the phone away. Okay. So, today we are going to continue with the, uh, with the second condition all, no sorry, the second conditional. We had the first conditional last week, you remember, if it rains, we will stay at home. That is real, that is possible. Today it is different. Today we are talking about things that are not real, things that are imaginary, or very unlikely. Okay?

So let me write it on the board. If I had a million dollars, comma, I would travel the world. Everybody see it? Dobře. Look at the structure. If, plus past simple, then comma, would plus infinitive. If I had, I would travel. That's the whole formula. If plus past simple, would plus infinitive.

Now, a Czech aside, because I know some of you are already confused. Je to vlastně jako kdyby v češtině: kdybych byl bohatý, koupil bych si velký dům. Vidíte? Kdybych byl, koupil bych. Ten pravý čas není minulý, i když to v angličtině vypadá jako past simple. It is not about the past. It is about imagination. Takže "had" tady neznamená, že se to stalo včera. It means it is not real now.

Yes, Terezo, you have a question?

Student: Is it, is it like, uh, if I will have, no, if I would have a million?

Exactly, that is exactly the mistake I wanted to talk about, thank you. Very important. Poslouchejte všichni. Nikdy neříkáme would v if-části. Never. Nikdy. Not "if I would have a million dollars". No no no. It is "if I had". The wood, the would, goes only in the second part, in the main clause. If I had, I would. Not if I would, I would. Okay? Tohle je nejčastější chyba, kterou vidím v testech, každý rok, každý rok, a pak mám smutné oči.

Student: A to platí i u toho, jako, I'd?

Good question. I'd, the short form, can be I would or I had, so be careful. If I'd known, that is a different thing, that is the third conditional, we will do that in spring, don't panic. Today just if I had, I'd go. Fine.

Let's have more examples. If I were you, I would study more. Now this is interesting. Look, I wrote were. If I were you. Not "was". Some of you will say, but teacher, I was, he was, she was. Yes, normally. But in the second conditional we can use were for all persons. If I were, if he were, if she were, if it were, if we were. In formal English, it is actually better, it is more correct. People say if I was, in speaking, a lot, and nobody will arrest you, but in the test, please, were. Takže v češtině je to něco jako "kdybych byl", u všech osob je to stejné "by", jenom se mění koncovka. Anglicky is simple, were for everyone. Easier than Czech, for once! Angličtina je jednodušší, zapište si to, nestává se to často.

Okay, let's practise. I will say the beginning and you finish. If I were a bird... Come on, somebody. Yes, Martine.

Student: I would fly to, to Italy.

Nice. I would fly to Italy. Why Italy, why not Slovakia? Okay, joke. Next. If I won the lottery... Anička?

Student: I would buy a, a horse.

A horse. Why a horse? I mean, fine, good, grammatically perfect, I would buy a horse. Where would you keep the horse? Na balkoně? Okay, okay, tak pojďme dál.

Now another thing. If we want to ask a question, we say what would you do if you saw a ghost? What would you do. Would you run away? Would you scream? Say it with your neighbour. Two minutes. Go.

...

Okay, okay, stop, stop, I hear some very creative answers in the back. Pavle, what did you say? You would invite the ghost for a beer? Well, that is polite, that's, that's very Czech. Good.

Now, the second part of the lesson. Wish. We use wish plus past simple when we want something to be different now. I wish I had more time. I wish I were taller. I wish I lived in Prague, for those who commute. Význam: přál bych si, aby... Mám pocit, že nemám dost času, ale ve skutečnosti ho nemám. The situation is not real, so we use the past. Same logic as with the second conditional. I wish I had a car, but I don't have a car. I wish it weren't raining, but it is raining. Okay?

And again, with wish, we also say I wish I were, not I wish I was, even if you can hear it in songs. Songs are not grammar books. Taylor Swift is not your teacher. I am your teacher, unfortunately.

Student: Can we say I wish I would have?

No. Same mistake. I wish I had. No wood, no would. Wood is for tables. Haha. Dobře, ten vtip byl špatný, I know, I know. Write it down anyway, wish plus past simple.

So let's do a quick exercise, just on the board. Complete the sentences. Number one: If I ... more money, I ... a new bike. Somebody. Dan?

Student: If I had more money, I would buy a new bike.

Perfect. Number two: If she ... here, she ... help us. Yes?

Student: If she was here, she would help us.

Almost, almost. What did we say about was? Were. If she were here, she would help us. Nobody is angry, we just correct it. Number three: If we ... a garden, we ... have a dog. Tereza?

Student: If we had a garden, we would have a dog.

Super. Perfect. See, you can do it. It's not rocket science, it's just a pattern.

Now let me tell you something, a small story. When I was at university, I had a teacher, an old British lady, and she always said, if I were the queen, I would abolish Mondays. And every Monday we said, yes, we agree, yes. That is a good second conditional. Imaginary, impossible, funny. So you can use it also for jokes. Like, if I were you, I would not eat that sandwich. Okay? Jirko, what is in the sandwich? Never mind.

Also, one more use. Advice. If I were you, I would study more. This is a polite way of giving advice. If I were you, I'd talk to him. If I were you, I wouldn't go there. Do you see? Radíte někomu, ale nejste příliš přísní. It is softer than "you must" or "you should". Native speakers love it.

Okay. Now, vocabulary. I need to tell you about the vocabulary test, so please write this down, don't just look at me. We have a vocabulary test next Thursday. Next Thursday. On unit five words. Unit five. The words you need to know: reluctant, r-e-l-u-c-t-a-n-t, reluctant, that is neochotný. Then afford, to afford, mít na něco peníze, dovolit si. Then behaviour, b-e-h-a-v-i-o-u-r, British spelling, with the u. Chování. And nowadays, v dnešní době, dneska. Reluctant, afford, behaviour, nowadays. Those four are the ones I am giving you as a list, but there are more in the unit, everything in the green box on page, I think, 58 and 59. Jo, 58 and 59. Everything in the green box.

And you can use them in the second conditional, of course. If I were reluctant, I wouldn't go. If I could afford it, I would buy it. Nowadays, nobody can afford a house in Prague, so that's, that's realistic, that is not a conditional, that's just life. Haha. Sorry. Sorry.

Student: Is the test, like, written, or oral?

Written. Written, twenty minutes at the beginning of the lesson. So don't come late. Honzo, I am looking at you, don't come late.

Now homework. Open your workbooks, please. Workbook, page sixty-four, exercise three. Sixty-four, three. It's the gap fill with the second conditional. And then, second part of the homework, write six sentences, six, with "If I were..." Six sentences, each one starting with If I were. For example, If I were the president, I would lower the price of beer. Haha, okay, maybe something more serious. If I were a teacher, I would never give homework. Hm, that's, that's a good one. Please, not exactly that one. Be creative. Six sentences, if I were, and the second part with would. Don't forget would in the main clause. And not in the if clause. Remember. Nikdy would v if-části.

Student: Do we hand it in?

Yes, hand it in on Monday, I will check it. Or send me by email, but print is better, my eyes, you know.

Okay. We have about five minutes left. Let's do one last game. I say a situation and you say what you would do. Situation: you find a wallet on the street, with a thousand euros. What would you do? Nobody? Okay, I will take them to the police, I think. Yes? Martin says he would keep it, hm, Martine, we need to talk after the class. Joke! Joke.

All right, to summarize. If plus past simple, would plus infinitive. Were for all persons. Wish plus past simple. No would in the if part. Homework: workbook sixty-four, exercise three, six sentences with If I were. Test next Thursday, unit five, reluctant, afford, behaviour, nowadays. Okay? Dobře. Thank you, see you on Monday, bye bye, have a nice day, and don't forget your workbooks. Hej, kdo nechal tu mikinu? Ne, to není moje.
traps: Homework part 2: write 6 sentences starting 'If I were...' with would in main clause
Homework to be handed in Monday (print preferred or email)
Vocabulary test next Thursday, unit 5, written, 20 minutes at start of lesson
Test word list: reluctant, afford, behaviour, nowadays (with Czech meanings neochotný, dovolit si, chování, v dnešní době)
Teacher says all unit 5 words in green box on pages 58 and 59 (unsure: 'I think, 58 and 59')
ASR error: 'second condition all' instead of 'second conditional' (teacher also self-corrects)
'would' heard as 'wood' twice: 'The wood, the would, goes only...' and 'No wood, no would'
Czech asides: kdybych byl bohatý, koupil bych si velký dům
Czech warning: Nikdy neříkáme would v if-části (not 'if I would have')
Rule: were for all persons in second conditional, 'was' tolerated in speech but not in test
Wish + past simple: I wish I had more time / I wish I were taller
Student mistake 'If she was here' corrected to 'were'
If I'd known = third conditional, to be taught in spring
Missing/wrong diacritics in some Czech words (e.g. 'Dobře' ok, 'Jo', 'neochotný') where ASR dropped them; Czech words partly without diacritics
Teacher jokes: horse on balcony, ghost beer, Taylor Swift not your teacher, wallet with thousand euros
Teacher says 'Taky' vs 'Tak pojďme dál' classroom management phrase used after the horse joke
Digression: British university teacher who would abolish Mondays
Spelling of 'behaviour' is British with u
